title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
directAnswer: Return the first index where `needle` appears in `haystack`, or −1. The simple answer is a sliding window: try each start `i` from 0 to n−m and compare the m-character window to needle — O(n·m) worst case. The optimal is KMP, which precomputes needle's longest-prefix-suffix (LPS) array to skip redundant rechecks, giving O(n + m).

remember.pattern: Substring search: brute window vs KMP prefix-function
remember.formula:
Brute: for i in 0..n-m: if haystack[i:i+m] == needle: return i
KMP: build lps[] of needle, then scan haystack with two pointers,
     on mismatch jump j = lps[j-1] instead of restarting
rules: **Only starts `0 … n − m` are viable** — past that, needle can't fit. Looping to `n` risks an out-of-bounds compare.
**Empty needle returns 0** by convention (it occurs at the start). Handle it before indexing.
**KMP never moves the haystack pointer backward** — that's the whole point; the LPS array tells you how far the matched prefix can be reused.
**The LPS array is built from needle alone**, independent of haystack, in O(m).
**On a KMP mismatch with `j > 0`, set `j = lps[j−1]`** and re-test the same haystack char — do NOT advance `i`.
whenToUse: Find the first (or any) occurrence of a pattern inside a larger string
The pattern is fixed and you may search it in one or many texts (precompute LPS once)
You need a guaranteed linear-time match, not just average-case
You want to avoid the quadratic blow-up of naive rechecking on repetitive text
antiSignals: You need ALL occurrences with overlaps → KMP still works but you continue instead of returning
Multiple different patterns at once → Aho–Corasick, not single-pattern KMP
Fuzzy/approximate match → edit-distance DP, not exact substring search
Tiny inputs where O(n·m) is trivially fine → brute force is cleaner to write under time pressure
remember.takeaway: Substring search is the canonical place to show you know KMP. Brute force re-checks overlapping windows and degrades to O(n·m) on repetitive strings like 'aaaaab'. KMP's prefix function records how much of needle is *already matched* so the text pointer never backtracks — turning it into O(n + m).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can write a correct windowed brute force AND whether you know that KMP (or another linear matcher) exists and why it's faster — even if you don't write KMP flawlessly from memory.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Off-by-one in the start bound (looping i to n instead of n − m), mishandling the empty needle, or claiming O(n) for brute force when it's O(n·m).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Write the clean brute force, state its O(n·m) worst case on repetitive input, then explain KMP's LPS idea — 'the text pointer never moves backward' — and ideally code it correctly. Mention Rabin–Karp as a hashing alternative.

problemStatement: Given two strings `needle` and `haystack`, return the index of the **first occurrence** of `needle` in `haystack`, or `-1` if `needle` is not part of `haystack`.
constraints: haystack and needle consist of only lowercase English characters
understanding: We're doing exact substring search: locate where the pattern (needle) starts inside the text (haystack). The brute force checks every possible alignment; the optimization (KMP) avoids re-examining characters by remembering how much of needle has already matched.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should I return if needle is empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 0 by convention — the empty string occurs at index 0. Current constraints say needle length ≥ 1, but a robust solution still guards it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need the first occurrence specifically, or any?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The first. Scanning left to right and returning on the first full match gives the smallest index naturally.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can the strings be, and does worst-case matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 10⁴ each. Brute force is 10⁸ in the worst case (e.g. 'aaaa…ab'), which is borderline — KMP's O(n+m) is the safe answer if pressed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are overlaps relevant?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not for the first occurrence — we stop at the first full match. Overlaps only matter for counting all occurrences.

examples.explanation: "sad" occurs at index 0 and again at index 6; the first occurrence is index 0.
"bba" never matches; brute force re-checks every window, KMP skips ahead using the LPS.

diagrams.title: Brute force vs KMP on mismatch
diagrams.caption: Brute force rewinds the text pointer; KMP keeps it and rewinds only the pattern pointer via LPS.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Sliding Window Compare
approaches.whenToMention: State first. It's the obvious correct baseline and frames why KMP is an improvement.
hints: needle can only start at positions where it still fits. What's the last start index you need to try in a haystack of length n with a needle of length m?
For each candidate start i, compare the m characters of haystack starting at i against needle. Return i on a full match.
Bail out of the inner comparison at the first mismatched character and move the start forward by one. Return -1 if no start matches.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are up to n − m + 1 start positions, and each window comparison costs up to m character checks → O((n − m + 1)·m) = O(n·m) worst case. Only a couple of indices are stored → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal reading of the problem: try to align needle at each position in haystack and check whether it matches there. Slide a window of length `m` across haystack and compare.

**Why the start index stops at `n − m`.** If needle has length `m`, it can only fit if there are at least `m` characters remaining. So the last viable start is `n − m`; any later and the window runs off the end of haystack. Writing the outer loop as `i from 0 to n − m` (inclusive) both covers every real candidate and prevents an out-of-bounds read inside the comparison. **Looping `i` all the way to `n` is the classic off-by-one that crashes or mis-compares.**

**Why we bail at the first mismatch.** For each start `i`, we compare character by character: `haystack[i + j]` against `needle[j]`. The moment they differ, this alignment is dead, so we stop the inner loop immediately and advance `i`. Only if the inner loop runs the full `m` characters without a mismatch (`j == m`) have we found a complete occurrence, and since we scan starts left to right, the first such `i` is the first occurrence.

**Why the worst case is quadratic.** Consider `haystack = "aaaaaaaaab"` and `needle = "aaab"`. At almost every start the first few characters match before failing on the final `b`, so each of the ~n windows does ~m work before bailing — `O(n·m)` total. For `n = m = 10⁴` that's `10⁸` comparisons, which is on the edge of acceptable. This redundancy — re-comparing characters we already looked at — is exactly what KMP eliminates. So brute force is the right thing to *say first*, but be ready to explain or write the linear-time version.
approaches.insight: Brute force re-examines the same haystack characters across overlapping windows; the work it wastes on repetitive input is precisely the inefficiency KMP removes by remembering matched prefixes.

approaches.name: KMP — Prefix Function (Optimal, O(n + m))
approaches.whenToMention: The linear-time answer. Lead with the idea — 'precompute how much of needle is a prefix that's also a suffix, so the text pointer never backtracks' — then code it.
hints: When a mismatch happens after matching a prefix of needle, you already KNOW those matched characters. Some suffix of that matched part might itself be a prefix of needle — could you reuse it instead of restarting?
Precompute, for each position in needle, the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix (the LPS / prefix-function array). This depends only on needle.

Scan haystack with pointer i (never decreases) and needle pointer j. On match, advance both; if j reaches m you found it. On mismatch with j > 0, set j = lps[j-1] and re-test haystack[i]; if j == 0, advance i.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the LPS array is O(m): the inner index only moves backward via lps and the build pointer advances monotonically, so amortized O(m). The search is O(n): the haystack pointer i never moves backward, and j decreases only via lps jumps that are bounded by the increases. Total O(n + m) time, O(m) for the LPS array.
approaches.explanation:
KMP (Knuth–Morris–Pratt) removes the redundancy in brute force. When brute force hits a mismatch after matching, say, 5 characters, it throws away all that knowledge and restarts one position over. KMP asks a smarter question: *of the characters I just matched, is some suffix also a prefix of needle?* If so, that suffix is already aligned and I can resume from there without re-reading haystack.

**The LPS array is the engine.** For each index `j` in needle, `lps[j]` is the length of the longest *proper* prefix of `needle[0..j]` that is also a suffix of it. For `needle = "aabaa"`, `lps = [0,1,0,1,2]`: the prefix `"aa"` at the end matches the prefix `"aa"` at the start, so `lps[4] = 2`. This table is computed from needle alone in `O(m)` using two pointers — a build pointer `i` that advances, and a `length` pointer that falls back via `lps[length-1]` on mismatch. **The key invariant: `length` is always the length of the current longest prefix-suffix.**

**Why the haystack pointer never moves backward.** During the search we keep `i` (into haystack) and `j` (into needle). On a match we advance both. On a mismatch with `j > 0`, instead of rewinding `i`, we set `j = lps[j-1]` — meaning 'the first `j` characters can't help, but the first `lps[j-1]` of them are already a valid matched prefix because they're both a prefix and a suffix of what we matched'. We then re-test `haystack[i]` against the new, shorter `needle[j]`. Only when `j == 0` and we still mismatch do we advance `i`. Because `i` is monotonic and never decreases, the search is `O(n)` — each haystack character is consumed at most once forward.

**Why this matters on repetitive input.** On `haystack = "aaaaaaaaab"`, `needle = "aaab"`, brute force re-scans the run of `a`s at every start. KMP, after a mismatch on `b`, falls `j` back via the LPS to skip exactly the characters it already knows match, so it sweeps the haystack once. That's the difference between `O(n·m)` and `O(n + m)`. Even if you can't reproduce KMP perfectly in an interview, articulating *why* it's linear — 'the text pointer never backtracks because the prefix function tells me how much I can reuse' — is what distinguishes a strong candidate.
approaches.insight: The prefix function answers, in O(1) per mismatch, 'how much of what I matched is reusable?'. Reusing the already-matched prefix-that-is-also-a-suffix is what lets the text pointer march forward monotonically — the single idea behind KMP's linearity.

diagrams.title: LPS-driven fallback keeps the text pointer still
diagrams.caption: On mismatch KMP shrinks j via lps[j-1]; the haystack pointer a only ever advances.

edgeCases.behavior: Text exhausts before j reaches m → returns -1, with no backtracking.
Where brute force is quadratic, KMP sweeps once via LPS fallbacks → O(n+m).

pitfalls: Advancing the haystack pointer on a mismatch when j > 0 — that defeats KMP and can skip a valid start.
Building LPS with length reset to 0 on mismatch instead of length = lps[length-1] — produces a wrong table.
Off-by-one in return: it's a - j (or i - j), not a.
Forgetting the empty-needle guard before indexing needle[0].

commonMistakes: Looping the start index to n instead of n − m, causing out-of-bounds or wasted work.
Not handling the empty needle (should return 0).
Calling brute force O(n) — it is O(n·m) worst case.
In KMP, moving the haystack pointer on a mismatch with j > 0 instead of falling back via lps[j−1].

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one in the start bound
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Looping i past n − m reads haystack[i + j] out of bounds during the window compare.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Backtracking the text pointer in KMP
commonMistakesDetailed.why: KMP's linearity depends on the haystack pointer never decreasing. Advancing it on a j>0 mismatch both breaks the invariant and can miss the true first occurrence.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong LPS build fallback
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Resetting length to 0 on a build mismatch discards reusable prefix-suffix info and yields an incorrect table, breaking the search.

followupVariations.title: Repeated Substring Pattern
followupVariations.hint: Solvable directly from the LPS array: the string is a repeat iff n % (n - lps[n-1]) == 0 and lps[n-1] > 0.

followupVariations.title: Shortest Palindrome
followupVariations.hint: Build the prefix function of needle + '#' + reverse(needle) to find the longest palindromic prefix.

followupVariations.title: Repeated String Match
followupVariations.hint: Repeat haystack enough times, then run KMP to test whether needle fits.

patternNote: Exact substring search. Brute force slides an m-window for O(n·m); KMP precomputes needle's prefix function (LPS) so the text pointer never backtracks, giving O(n+m). The LPS idea also powers Repeated Substring Pattern and Shortest Palindrome. Rabin–Karp (rolling hash) is the hashing-based alternative.
